review: Do you like old school Zelda?  Want to play something similar?  This does a fantastic job scratching that itch.

I purchased both of these games in a bundle. I bought them because they really look like Zelda. 

This review may change, as I contnue to TRY to give this game it's fais shake, but I'm not impressed.

Oddly enough, the primary issue of this game is displayed right there in the trailer. Some Grand Children approach their sleeping Grandfather to tell them a story. And then the Grandfather begins to tell the story that you play. So we've immediately broken the fourth wall, and even within the fiction we witness between the Grand Children and the Grand Father is ANOTHER fiction of Lilly the Knighted Warrior. 

So... this is a fiction within a fiction... Weird. 

Remember the movie "The Princess Bride"? There's momments when the little boy interjects into the story and the Grandfather explains things. In that movie, it worked, because it was rare, funny, and somehow didn't effect the narrative... but that happens in this game. The narrator and his two audience members interjecting into the story. The Grandfather forgetting details, and then you get to choose if you fight archers or golemns... because Grandpa's memory is crap... This narrative style keeps reminding me that I'm playing a fiction within a fiction. The unreliable memory of the Narrator DOES offer me choices, when playing the game, which is usually a good thing, but in this case, it just reminds me that I'm playing a fiction within a fiction. 

When playing this game, the story seems so primatively constructed, racing from one thing to the next... that I don't care. 

The music is okay. The trailer grabbed me because of the graphic… look like Zelda, and the music seemed highly inspired by it.

Sure the graphics are inspired by Zelda, that becomes less significant once you realize that it doesn't control like Zelda. The feel isn't entirely wrong, but it's far from feeling familiar. This interplay between graphics and controls gets a 5/10.

From what I can see, so far, there's only one song track that sounds similar to Zelda, and that's the one that plays in the Trailer, you know... the one that sounds like The Fairy Fountain. And that's great and all, but all th: other musical tracks I've heard aren't as derrivative and are independantly written. That's nice and all. I wouldn't want the entire game to just be derrivative... but what's truly new, in the musical arena, for this game, isn't really as compellig, I give the music a 4/10

I'll keep playing it, but as of right now, this game AS A WHOLE gets a 3/10 from me. I'm not impressed at all. I hate the Grand Children. I hate the Grandfather. Much of their dialogue could be character dialogue between characters in the  game you're ACTUALLY interacting with, and some of it is just really on-the-nose, explaining things as a tutorial. That's stupid. The developers should take notes from Hyperlight Drifter.

Don’t really have much to say other than it’s a good LoZ clone. You got dungeons You got a world to explore with sidequests, mini games and secrets. And the music and graphics look good. However I don’t have much else to talk about that isn't an annoyance so I’ll just say if you like LoZ clones cause you don’t like the real deal for some reason like me, go ahead and get it. And maybe its sequel, I haven’t played that one yet. Okay.Okay. Now…

-Why is there no gender select. Usually this is a non-issue but the set up is that this is a story told to a pair of twins by their grandfather. One boy and one girl. And the player character is Lily, the girl twin. Why no boy twin option? I know it doesn’t matter since Lily isn’t a character but it’s the easiest and obvious way to get a feature like that in.
-The sword kind of sucks after the first dungeon. Sure it’s fine for puzzles and cutting grass, but after getting weapons like the bow, bombs and boomerang, two of which can be upgraded, and some late game spells like the fire shield or lightning storm, why would you ever use the sword. Sure at the end you can shoot lasers but only at full health.
-Okay, I like the puzzles…Except those singing stones ones. The optional ones can get annoying long with one I had to cheat by recording video of the sequences.
-The mini bosses felt harder than the regular bosses for some reason. With the exceptions of the rat king and golem, all the boss fights were ‘hit it until it dies’. But the mini bosses either felt like they had more health or were just harder to hit.

That’s my list of complaints. Still a good game which I can recommend.

Blossom Tales is a charming indie pixel art game that offers a concise and enjoyable experience, taking roughly 14 hours to achieve 100 percent completion.

The game uses a sweet bedtime story as its narrative foundation, which adds a unique layer of personality to the adventure.

However, from a completionist perspective, the game can be frustrating because it lacks a clear tracking system for missing items. The map itself is unfortunately quite difficult to read, and it would have been a great improvement if completed objectives were clearly marked on it. This lack of oversight makes it exceptionally difficult to use guides during the endgame, as there is no easy way to identify which specific secrets are still outstanding.

Additionally, the inventory system feels a bit unorganized since it lacks fixed slots, items are simply added in the order you find them, which makes scrolling through your gear quite tedious. 
It also would have been a significant quality-of-life improvement if the game allowed players to map more than just two items at a time for quicker access during gameplay.

The game's cool, but some design choices worsened my experience, and these may bother you if you're picky like me.

Controller customizability:
It lets you assign items and gear to A, B and X. For instance, the sword could be assigned to X, the shield to A and the shovel to B. The thing is: It doesn't let you assign them to other buttons, such as RB, which would be nice for the shield, for instance. You do have the option to force RB to work as A via Steam Input, but the game's own interface doesn't adapt to it, of course, and it gets a bit confusing when you need to press the A button, yet it's you're pressing RB instead.

Item descriptions:
When you find a new item or piece of gear, the game gives you a brief description of it. The problem is: It never shows this description again, neither does it show the object's name, so it can get a bit confusing after a while.

Dialogue:
The game lets you check every previous piece of dialogue, or documents that the protagonist has read before. Literally everything. The bad part about it is that it's all a huge text, which is thankfully separated by dialogues, but you just scroll through it all. There's no way of filtering it, searching for key words, or even choosing between dialogues that took place in one part of the kingdom or another, which is a really bad choice.

-----

My verdict is that the game is cool, the gameplay and story seemed good overall, but those design choices that I spoke of made it unpleasant to my taste, which is why I stopped playing the game and don't recommend it.

I was going to 100% this, but it's so boring and aggravating that I just can't and won't.
It didn't take long to start disliking this when I first booted it up. Seriously... it was less than 30 minutes, when I started dreading this. I could have turned it off and refunded it as I just knew it wasn't going to get better, but for some reason I wanted to annoy myself and decided to play until the end. I was going to try and explore everything but after a couple hours, I couldn't be bothered and then just decided to get through the game as quickly as I could.
The controls are so wonky and you cannot configure them. I played with keyboard. You move with the arrow keys, you attack with Z, and the two item/tool buttons are X and C. You interact with NPCs and furniture/signs with Z. So you may swing your sword instead of interacting with something, or vice versa. Lily controls weirdly and hitboxes are sometimes wonky.
I did not really like any of the music, especially the freaking castle town music, which was getting on my nerves and giving me a headache. (I had to turn down the music volume a lot.)
Every item uses the stamina/energy/magic meter (Whatever it's called.) Yes, the bombs and bow. There's no quantity to arrows or bombs, even the boomerang uses the meter, you just have to wait and let the meter recharge to use the items again.

The side quests are just "Fetch" quests, As in a character wants 20 of whatever they ask of you and you have to go kill the mob that drops it over and over again until you get the 20 materials and then bring it back to them. The material does not drop from every single mob, so you will more than likely have to kill more than 20 of the specific enemy type. So although it shouldn't take very long considering you can easily reset the enemies by leaving the room/zone and then enter it again, it's kinda tedious and boring, and two(?) defend the NPC for a minute or so from small waves of enemies quests. OH and a deliver the mail to a specific NPC in a specific area quest. You have to do this like 7 or 6 times. (Very boring and tedious in this game.) You get an achievement if you complete the whole quest, but I didn't because the last person you have to deliver to is the the traveling merchant guy who's apparently only available between 9AM-5PM REAL TIME!

The writing of both the story and dialogue is very childish, which obviously means this game is meant for kids, but then there's the terrible controls, the repetitive and semi-annoying puzzles (especially the singing stones puzzles), the bullet hell-like damage sponge boss fights, and the rage-inducing crumbling pathways/bridges. There's a really annoying secret basement in one of the "towns" where the challenge is a narrow crumbling pathway/bridge that goes on for too long, and if you fall, it sends you back to the beginning of the room. (I also can't imagine kids wanting to play random indie games, let alone pixel indie games. If they're into the graphics and old-school games, then they're just going to play the iconic/classic/popular old games.) So the age rating is kinda all over the place.

A random NPC literally says: "I'm Jennifer, or Jen for short. Or J Dawg, J Drizzle, J to the Pizzo, Little J, Jiggy J, Jay J, whatevs."

Why?

The "About The Game" section of the game's page lists these "Features":

"15+ hours of gameplay" - (This is only true if you do the boring side content / go for 100%. Otherwise, the main story is less than 6 hours. A couple of my hours are AFK hours.)

"Huge, diverse game world with many different locations" - (I feel like this sentence is kinda a lie. Sure the world is kinda big (Not huge), but your character (Lily) gets stuck/slowed down on a lot of a lot of crap, making you traverse the map a lot slower. And it's not really diverse with "many" different locations. Most of them are pretty empty and are practically just the same as the previous zone.)

"5 challenging dungeons" - (Boring, straightforward and way too long? Yes. Challenging? No.)

"Various items impacting gameplay and fighting style" - (There weren't a TON of different items, despite what some reviewers say, but anyways, there's really not much reason to use them other than the bombs and your sword.)

"Fun, charming storytelling" - (No. It got old quick, and the characters (Grandpa, Lily and Chrys) story "interruptions" felt pointless and kinda broke the immersion. Also why did the game have to spell Chris like that... and I'm surprised Chrys didn't care that Grandpa put his sister in the story, making her the hero, and didn't feel the need to put Chrys in it lol.)

This is not worth the $15 price tag. I got it for $4 and I can't even recommend it at that price. I really wanted to play more zelda-like/clones, which, I mean, I did, this is very obviously inspired by TLoZ, but it all felt a bit "off", like I was playing a custom game on Warcraft 3. (Weird, I know, but it just gave me those vibes.)

Decent classic TLoZ clone with some baffling design decisions. It's a good game for Steam Deck.

·The story is a tale that Grandpa narrates to his two grandchildren, with one of them as the protagonist, and it changes depending on how he feels or the kids react, and sometimes gives you an option to select what happens next. When you load a savegame there is a segment where Grandpa goes "Where were we?..." and gives a recap. It's cute.

·There are many small side quests and secrets. All of them fetch quests and very obvious bomb cracks or hidden holes in the ground.
·Settings are very limited. At least there is Steam Cloud Support.
·Music was surprisingly enjoyable, but audio mixing could be better, some trap sounds are way louder that other sounds.
·I get what the inspiration is but the movement speed feels too low for an exploration game and there is no upgrade other than a dash item that consumes meter, has very low range, and kills your momentum afterwards.
·You also don't get a "teleport whenever you want" item until you beat the game and the fixed teleport locations are not always at the best places.
·Edge detection near pitfalls and falling floors feels iffy. Don't even try to play with joystick, use d-pad.
·There is something weird with the way the game does the pick/throw items and direct bomb throwing. It's like if you press diagonal it sometimes does not work properly. Again, don't bother with a joystick, it feels bad.
·There is a gimmick with a merchant that only appears at working hours. Either you don't have work to do or they force you to change the system clock. Hate that kind of design choice to be honest.


The thing I disliked the most about the game is the difficulty and design inconsistency. It's like they couldn't decide what the target audience was:
 ·They tell you where to go next in the map. You simply can't get lost if you don't want to.
 ·They give you way too many hearts too early. I had 10 hearts for the second dungeon boss fight.
 ·I believe there isn't a single damage source that doesn't deal more that half a heart. You can tank long lava corridors and any trap like you are invincible. There is no challenge at all in exploration.
 ·They give you potions that heal all your hearts and auto-revive items like candy. There are also potions that straight up make you invincible for a time if you use them.
 ·There are no consumable weapons to manage. Everything is tied to a meter that regenerates constantly.

But then:
 ·The bosses are almost bullet-hell, HP sponges, with fast near undodgeable attacks sometimes (not that it matters).
 ·Obtuse puzzle that could be interpreted in many ways and so you either have to check the solution somewhere or brute force it.
 ·Randomized memory puzzles that reset after every mistake AND correct answer. This wouldn't be a bad thing if not for the fact that they are TEN layers deep and you have to do it all over again if you fail and it doesn't give you any time to take notes. There is no way that a young player is going to be able to complete this kind of thing, as it is hard even for adults.
 ·Some but not all of the other kind of puzzles (sliding blocks) also feel harder than they should be.
 ·There are segments with narrow falling platforms and player tracking projectile traps that are a complete nightmare. I gave up at one of these in the last dungeon because it was feeling miserable and not worth the time anymore.

So is the target audience young kids that might have difficulty completing basic challenges? Or is it adults that know what they are doing? Either way the game feels like it wasn't bad enough to drop but also not enjoyable overall. One of these that are there just to pass the time.

It is hard to recommend this game. But if you want a 2D zelda-like you might still enjoy it. 

On the bright side, you get a bunch of cool tools to play with : aside from bow boomerang and bombs you get medallions that summon earthquakes, thunder, or just a swarm of homing bees (this one's great), and some other things. The story is basic but told in a charming way. The musics are alright, sometimes good. The visuals are nice as well. The first biome and first dungeon have nice design and atmosphere, and a cast of interesting enemies. The puzzles are classic but there's enough variety in the dungeon rooms that its length isn't much of a problem. 
And then it stops. 
After the first dungeon, the game just starts to turn into an enemy spam slog. Each room, be it overworld or dungeons, starts being crowded by 15+ mobs (fun fact, they all respawn each time you leave the room) and few points of interest. The diversity in enemies and puzzles plummets, the item you get in dungeons 2 and 3 feels much less interesting in the level design and combat design than the first one. In the last dungeon there were 3 different mobs of a same family and I honestly can't really tell what difference they had in gameplay. Even some of the puzzles stopped being well-thought and were just based on a geometric pattern, itreally felt to me the devs wanted to get the game out and nothing else.
I didn't like the character controller very much, the sword's hitbox often feels more situational than it should and my character often ignores my prompts to turn around to hit something else. There's a map that isn't super useful, considering each square area of the map is about 4 times your game camera, and each has several exits, so you often spend much longer exploring than you would need to because you try out each exit of a room and find out they lead back to the same previous one. I was also a bit frustrated by the lack of uses for money late game and the rare use for potions, which you get by the dozen, because the game has a lot of chests to find but it doesn't have anything to give beside money and potions.

Basically, my first 3 hours of gameplay were very enjoyable despite a few flaws, and the 7 remaining ones drained me slowly of the hope the game was going to get back on its feet. If you don't mind fighting lots of mobs or just constantly ignoring them as you go through rooms you should have a better time than me.

I understand that I'm probably not the target audience which I believe would be up to about 12 years old. 

There's really nothing wrong with the game, but to be fair there's nothing really good either. The story is alright, the graphics are ok, the sound is decent. But in the end nothing stands out. The puzzles aren't even puzzles (I don't think I needed more than one try for any of them). The whole game is basically just walking around to different spots that pose no challenge or change of pace of any sort. 

For the most part I couldn't even be arsed to dodge the lava or the snowballs and just tanked them and the same goes for all the fights (including bosses). So if you're looking for a challenge, some new take on anything; this is not where you'll find it. 

If you are a child, or if you have a kid, and they think The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past is fun but too difficult - this might be the solution to ease them in. Otherwise I see no reason to buying this,. 

TL;DR: "But we've got Zelda at home..."

Я слишком давно играл в The Legend of Zelda, чтобы подтвердить, что в Blossom Tales из какой части Зельды слизано под копирку, как утверждают в некоторых других обзорах. Но ощущение вторичности вполне естественно может возникнуть даже без свежих воспоминаний о Зельде: Blossom Tales не просто вдохновлён Зельдой, а чистый клон, старающийся подражать оригиналу практически во всём. Подражает с переменным успехом: если к визуалу и способностям персонажа вопросов нет, то ко всему остальному они возникают. В целом головоломки и испытания неплохи, но некоторые либо вызывают недоумение неожиданно сложным вызовом к памяти или ловкости игрока, либо изредка вопрос, а что вообще у разработчика в голове. Побочные квесты часто представляют собой гринд ресурсов с монстров. Звуковое сопровождение нередко вызывает некоторое раздражение. Прогрессия выстроена таким образом, что сложность боёв с чего-то на уровне Зельды в начале скатывается до практически бессмертия к середине игры, а то и раньше, из-за обилия зелий и цветков воскрешения (умереть можно, но сложно), хотя конечно это можно счесть и за плюс в зависимости от предпочтений. Идея представить повествование как рассказ деда своим внукам вызывает некоторое умиление, выражающееся в виде изредка появляющейся лёгкой улыбки, особенно когда дети вмешиваются в происходящее, но не более того — ни одной нормальной шутки, ни одного запоминающегося персонажа, ни одной интересной мысли в сюжете и диалогах.
Вообще, игра ни в чём не предлагает чего-то оригинального, чего-то своего. Но, надо отдать должное, копия вышла по большей части недурной. Если хочется, например, перепройти A Link To The Past, но в другой обёртке, Blossom Tales вполне может порадовать в течение 7-10 часов (15+ часов прохождения, как указано в описании, может набраться разве что если пытаться выполнить достижения на сбор всех предметов в игре). Во всех остальных случаях — проходите мимо.

This is more of a thumbs sideways, cause I'm really not too hot on this game, but I also don't think it's bad. Mainly, I think this game just cribs too much from Zelda without innovating on it enough or adding significant enough convenience features. Case-in-point: you still have to deal with the same inventory juggling from A Link to the Past where you have to constantly switch items into your action button slot to use them, and it sucks less only because your inventory is smaller. Also, a big thing with action adventure games like this: No map pins. You've got to remember where everything is yourself, or manually map it which sucks. It's one of the #1 things that keeps me from getting into 2D Zelda, and it's less bad here, again only because there's less to find and navigation is more straightforward. I mean, don't get me wrong, if you're into Zelda you'll probably like this at least a little. I've just played games far more interesting and innovative in the top down action adventure genre. Play UNSIGHTED, CrossCode, Anodyne 1 & 2, Prodigal, even Hyper Light Drifter before you play this. I'm probably still going to check out the sequel, but only when it goes on sale.

Blossom Tales: The Sleeping King is a wonderful game that offers quite a bit for its short playtime.  It is definitely a love letter to older Zelda games like Link to the Past, Link's Awakening, and the Oracle Series.  The music is great, the graphics are imaginative (I particularly like the clouds and the torches), and the story is endearing.  My only gripe is the lack of a more easily accessible fast travel option or a way to quickly exit dungeons.  Because the game saves every time the screen changes, if you reset the game from the main menu then you start on the same screen you ended the game on.  This is great if you are trying to complete the main quest, but it isn't so great if you are hunting for missed collectibles and just want to get out of a dungeon quickly.

However, I don't think this should dissuade anyone from getting this game.  Far from it.  It is a charming addition to any library. :)
